name: Dajia Zhenlan Temple
address: No. 158, Shuntian Rd, Dajia District, Taichung City
description: Every third lunar month, a single Mazu palanquin sets off on foot with hundreds of thousands of people behind it: nine days and eight nights, more than 300 kilometers through Taichung, Changhua, Yunlin, and Chiayi. This is Dajia Zhenlan Temple's Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage. Zhenlan Temple, in Dajia District, Taichung City, is dedicated to Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother). It is the best-known Mazu temple in Taiwan and a heartland of Taiwanese Mazu devotion. In the basement beneath its glittering halls sits the 'Golden Mazu,' a 276-kilogram figure cast from gold medallions that worshippers offered in thanks for answered prayers, and the temple's greatest treasure. If you want to feel the almost feverish devotion Taiwanese people have for Mazu, this is the place to start.
history: The story begins with a statue that crossed the sea. Tradition holds that in 1730, the eighth year of the Qing Yongzheng reign, Lin Yongxing, an immigrant from Meizhou in Fujian, brought a Mazu statue to Taiwan and settled in Dajia. That was the beginning of Zhenlan Temple. Over the next two centuries and more, the temple was expanded and rebuilt many times, and a major rebuilding in 1980 (the 69th year of the Republic of China calendar) gave its halls their grand scale of today. What truly made Dajia Mazu famous across Taiwan is the pilgrimage that has carried on year after year. Wherever the palanquin goes, whole towns pour into the streets; devotees crawl beneath it and reach out to steady its frame, hoping for a share of Mazu's protection. Today the pilgrimage is far more than a religious event. It gathers up the feelings of an entire society and has become the most vivid symbol of Taiwanese folk belief.

visit.whenToGo: The Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage in the 3rd lunar month each year is the highlight of the year: nine days and eight nights to Xingang Fengtian Temple in Chiayi and back, with huge crowds inside and outside the temple around the departure.

name: Beigang Chaotian Temple
address: No. 178, Zhongshan Rd, Beigang Township, Yunlin County
description: Say 'Beigang Mazu' and a thousand Mazu temples across Taiwan prick up their ears. Beigang Chaotian Temple, in Beigang Township, Yunlin County, is a heartland of Mazu devotion in Taiwan and the 'ancestral temple' that many other Mazu temples return to on pilgrimage. Its standing is so high that it is listed as a national historic monument. Dedicated to Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother), Chaotian Temple has branch temples all over the world. Every third lunar month, around Mazu's birthday, pilgrim groups from everywhere flood into this small town, with drums and gongs thundering and incense smoke curling through the air: 'Mazu fever' at its most intense. Inside, the stone carvings and cut-porcelain work preserve some superb Qing dynasty architectural art.
history: In 1694, the 33rd year of the Qing Kangxi reign, the Chan monk Shubi carried a Mazu statue across the sea from the Chaotian Pavilion on Meizhou and built a temple for it in Beigang. So began one of the oldest Mazu temples in Taiwan. During the Qing dynasty, Chaotian Temple repeatedly received imperial titles and plaques bestowed by the court, which raised it to great prominence. Over the centuries the temple was restored and expanded again and again, its cut-porcelain and koji pottery decoration growing ever more exquisite, until it became a national historic monument. Every year from the fifteenth day of the first lunar month through the third month, Mazu temples from all over Taiwan come here on pilgrimage, and the town is wrapped in incense smoke and the roar of drums and gongs. Then there is the 'palanquin bombing,' in which devotees set off huge quantities of firecrackers beneath the deity palanquins, one of the fiercest and most spectacular temple-festival scenes anywhere in Taiwan.

visit.whenToGo: From lunar 1/15 through the 3rd lunar month each year is the peak season for Mazu temples from around Taiwan to come on pilgrimage, and pilgrimage groups are most concentrated around Mazu's birthday on lunar 3/23.

name: Lugang Tianhou Temple
address: No. 430, Zhongshan Rd, Lukang Township, Changhua County
description: There is only one in all of Taiwan. Lugang Tianhou Temple, in Lugang Township, Changhua County, enshrines the founding Holy Mother statue from the Meizhou ancestral temple, and that is what it is proudest of. Dedicated to Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother), the temple's Mazu statue has been darkened to a glossy black by long years of incense smoke, so people affectionately call her 'Black-Faced Mazu.' The temple is grand and imposing, its wood and stone carvings the work of master craftsmen, and the 'bagua caisson ceiling' over the main hall is a treasure of Taiwanese craftsmanship. Step inside and you step into the faded glory captured in the old saying 'first Tainan, second Lugang, third Monga.' Every New Year, worshippers rush to light 'bright lamps' and perform the 'an tai sui' rite, and spots are often hard to get.
history: Lugang Tianhou Temple had already been built by 1683, the 22nd year of the Qing Kangxi reign. In 1725, the third year of the Yongzheng reign, Shi Shibang donated land and the temple moved to its present site, dedicated to the Heavenly Holy Mother. Lugang was then the largest trading port in central Taiwan; the saying 'first Tainan, second Lugang, third Monga' sums up its prosperity, and Tianhou Temple stood at the heart of the old streets, watching more than two hundred years of trade rise and fall. Under Japanese rule, a large-scale restoration began in 1927 and was completed in 1936, setting the layout you see today. Now the temple, Lugang Old Street, Moru Lane, and Jiuqu Lane together form a complete historic district, one of the best windows onto the culture of a Qing dynasty Taiwanese trading port.

visit.whenToGo: During the New Year, worshippers rush to light guangming lamps and perform Tai Sui rites, and spots are often hard to get; Mazu's birthday on lunar 3/23 is also an important day.

name: Baishatun Gongtian Temple
address: No. 8, Baidong Li, Tongxiao Township, Miaoli County
description: No one knows which way Mazu will go today, and that is exactly what makes Baishatun Gongtian Temple so captivating. This temple in Tongxiao Township, Miaoli County, is dedicated to a 'soft-bodied' Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother) and is one of the Mazu temples in Taiwan with the most personality. Its annual walking pilgrimage to Beigang Chaotian Temple has 'no fixed route': the direction is left entirely to the improvised guidance of Mazu's palanquin, nicknamed the 'Pink Supercar,' so the whole journey is full of mystery and surprise. The procession moves fast and urgently, and it often turns into schools, hospitals, or private homes to bless the people inside, scattering Mazu's warmth and compassion into ordinary households all along the way.
history: During the Qianlong reign, the early settlers of Baishatun brought a soft-bodied Mazu statue into a private home to worship. Late in the Xianfeng reign they pooled funds to build a temple, which was completed in 1863, the second year of the Tongzhi reign: the beginning of Gongtian Temple. The people here have made their living from the sea for generations, and faith in Mazu has been their most important spiritual anchor against wind and waves. What truly sets Baishatun Mazu apart is the pilgrimage that has carried on year after year: the palanquin travels on foot from Baishatun to Beigang Chaotian Temple in Yunlin, with the departure date chosen each year by casting divination blocks. In 2026 the journey took eight days and seven nights. Unlike Dajia Mazu, Baishatun Mazu decides her own route, pointing the way through the swaying of her palanquin, so the path is different every year, which is why she is hailed as 'the Mazu with the most personality.' The number of devotees following the palanquin grows every year; in 2026, registrations passed 460,000.

visit.whenToGo: It is liveliest during the annual walking pilgrimage to Beigang Chaotian Temple. The departure date is decided each year by casting moon blocks, so check the temple's announcements before you go.

name: Changhua Nanyao Temple
description: A Mazu temple that blends Japanese, Greek, and Baroque styles: that is the most striking sight at Changhua Nanyao Temple in Changhua City. Dedicated to Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother) and popularly known as 'Changhua Mazu,' Nanyao Temple has a main hall in the traditional southern Fujian style, while its rear hall, the Guanyin Hall, is strongly shaped by Western architecture. Such an East-meets-West mix is extremely rare among Taiwanese temples, and its artistic value is exceptional. Nanyao Temple also has ten Mazu associations, and its annual Bengang pilgrimage has a long history, preserving old rites such as the 'changing of the dragon robe.' It is a living fossil of Taiwan's pilgrimage culture.
history: The story begins with an incense pouch. Tradition says that during the Qing Yongzheng reign, a potter named Yang Qian carried a Mazu incense pouch with him for people to pray to. Its miracles were so striking that more and more believers gathered, until in 1738, the third year of the Qianlong reign, Nanyao Temple was built. The Changhua County Gazetteer of the Daoguang reign already records Nanyao Temple making its yearly pilgrimage to Bengang. From then on, the temple's devotee organizations, the 'Mazu associations,' kept growing, and their influence spread across central Taiwan. From one small incense pouch to ten Mazu associations, Nanyao Temple shows how Taiwan's pilgrimage culture grew out of folk belief into a force that binds a community together.

visit.whenToGo: The annual Bengang pilgrimage is a major tradition at Nanyao Temple; Mazu's birthday on lunar 3/23 is also the most important day for a Mazu temple.

name: Taichung Lecheng Temple
address: No. 48, Hanxi St, East District, Taichung City
description: The longest Mazu procession in Taiwan happens here: the Hanxi Mazu procession through eighteen villages lasts a full 22 days. Taichung Lecheng Temple, popularly called the 'Hanxi Mazu Temple,' stands in Taichung's East District. It was once one of Taichung's four great Mazu temples, is listed as a municipal historic site, and is dedicated to Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother). Its rebuilding was led by the master craftsman Chen Yingbin, and its wood and stone carvings are exquisite. Beyond Mazu's reputation for answering prayers, the temple's Yuelao Hall, devoted to the Old Man Under the Moon, is famous across Taiwan and hailed as 'the most efficacious Yuelao in central Taiwan.' Every year countless single people come to pray for a match, and it has brought together countless happy couples. Pray to Mazu and ask for a good match: here you can do both.
history: In 1753, the 18th year of the Qing Qianlong reign, the ancestors of Lin Dafa came to Hanxi to clear land and brought Mazu with them, and the villagers built a temple for her. This was the forerunner of Lecheng Temple. As the area was settled and grew, the temple was gradually enlarged and more deities were added, until it became the most important center of faith around Hanxi. Under Japanese rule, the temple engaged the master craftsman Chen Yingbin to lead a major rebuilding, which set its present architectural layout. In 2005, a Yuelao Hall was added on the second floor of the rear hall. The temple still preserves an altar table bearing a Jiaqing-era inscription and a 1904 plaque reading 'Fa Yu Hong Shi.' From a small temple on the banks of the Hanxi to a center of faith with unbroken incense and a procession through eighteen villages, Lecheng Temple has always been woven tightly into the everyday faith and community life of the people around it.

visit.whenToGo: The Hanxi Mazu procession through eighteen villages lasts 22 days and is the temple's main event of the year. Those seeking a match mostly come to pray at the Yue Lao hall around Qixi (lunar 7/7) and Valentine's Day on February 14.

name: Zhushan Zinan Temple
address: No. 40, Dagong St., Zhushan Township, Nantou County
description: Borrow NT$600 from the Earth God: that is what Zhushan Zinan Temple is best known for. This temple in Zhushan Township, Nantou County, is dedicated to Tudigong, the Earth God, and is famous across Taiwan for 'borrowing fortune money.' Worshippers borrow 600 from the Earth God as 'mother money' and tuck it into their wallets so their money will keep multiplying. If they have made a profit by the following year, they return the principal and add whatever incense donation they wish. Every Lunar New Year, crowds line up to borrow fortune money. The temple also built a public restroom called 'Golden Bamboo Shoot Welcomes Guests,' which has unexpectedly become an attraction in its own right.
history: In 1745, the tenth year of the Qing Qianlong reign, residents around Zhushan built a small shrine to the Earth God who protected their community. That was where Zinan Temple began. What truly made this little temple famous across Taiwan was the tradition of borrowing fortune money. Word spread that mother money borrowed from the Earth God was especially effective, and as the story passed from one person to the next, worshippers came from all over Taiwan and the incense burned brighter every year. The temple has put donations to good use, steadily improving its surroundings and facilities, until even the public restroom became a sight to see. And so a small shrine to the Earth God became the most important center of tourism and faith in Zhushan, Nantou.

visit.whenToGo: During the Lunar New Year, crowds of worshippers queue to borrow fortune money; the Earth God's birthday on lunar 2/2 is also an important day.

name: Songboling Shoutian Temple
address: No. 118, Songshan St, Mingjian Township, Nantou County
description: Stand on Songboling at the southern end of the Bagua Mountains and the plain below opens up before you: this is the 'Distant View from Songling' that belongs to Songboling Shoutian Temple alone. Located in Mingjian Township, Nantou County, Shoutian Temple is dedicated to Xuantian Shangdi (the Supreme Emperor of the Dark Heaven) and is one of the head ancestral temples of his worship in Taiwan. More than 18,000 temples and shrines have taken incense from it, and its incense burns exceptionally strong. Every year around Xuantian Shangdi's birthday on the third day of the third lunar month, pilgrim groups from all over Taiwan arrive in an endless stream, with lively, colorful troupe performances: one of the great events of Taiwan's religious calendar. A climb with a sweeping view and a visit to an ancestral temple in one trip make it well worth the journey.
history: Perched on Songboling at the southern end of the Bagua Mountains and dedicated to Xuantian Shangdi, Shoutian Temple traces its origins to 1657, the 11th year of the Ming Yongli reign, when settlers worshipped Xuantian Shangdi's incense in the mountain valleys. Only in 1737, the second year of the Qing Qianlong reign, was a small temple built on the present site. On the strength of its reputation for answering prayers, it grew into one of the most important ancestral temples of Xuantian Shangdi worship in Taiwan, and over the centuries its incense has been divided across the island to more than 18,000 temples. Xuantian Shangdi temples everywhere organize groups each year to return to Songboling and pay respects to the ancestral temple, forming an unbroken pilgrimage network. On the third day of the third lunar month, Xuantian Shangdi's birthday, drums and gongs thunder across the mountain and troupes gather, as pilgrims from all over Taiwan turn this ancestral temple into the liveliest religious festival in central Taiwan. The wide view from Songling and incense handed down through the generations have made Shoutian Temple a sacred place in the hearts of Xuantian Shangdi's devotees.

visit.whenToGo: Around Xuantian Shangdi's birthday on lunar 3/3, pilgrimage groups and performance troupes from all over Taiwan flood up to Songboling, making it the liveliest time of the year.

name: Beigang Wude Palace
address: No. 330, Huasheng Rd, Beigang Township, Yunlin County
description: When business people want to pray for wealth, they come here. Beigang Wude Palace, in Beigang Township, Yunlin County, is the founding ancestral temple of Taiwan's Five Directions Gods of Wealth and the largest of its kind in Taiwan. Dedicated to Zhao Gongming, the heavenly-official Martial God of Wealth, Wude Palace is a majestic complex with a 'Heavenly Treasury' furnace several stories tall, billed as the largest in the world, built for worshippers to burn 'treasury money' that replenishes their fortune. It is a must-visit for business owners and merchants, its incense burns extraordinarily strong, and the 'mother money' it hands out every New Year is very popular. Pray for wealth, top up your fortune, and collect your mother money, all in one stop.
history: Beigang Wude Palace is dedicated to Zhao Gongming, the heavenly-official Martial God of Wealth, who is the 'God of Wealth of the Center' commanding the Gods of Wealth of the five directions: east, west, south, north, and center. The temple's forerunner was the Baosheng Tang Chinese herbal medicine shop, opened in 1957. Wude Palace was formally founded in 1978, and its new temple was completed in 1980. Beigang has been a commercial hub of the Yunlin-Chiayi region since the Qing dynasty, and its traders held the Martial God of Wealth in special reverence, so the temple's incense burned ever brighter. Known widely as 'the founding ancestral temple of the Five Directions Gods of Wealth,' Wude Palace became one of the most famous wealth-god temples in Taiwan. In the main hall, Zhao Gongming is enshrined as the Martial God of Wealth of the Center, with the Gods of Wealth of the east, west, south, and north on either side. On the fifteenth day of the third lunar month, the Martial God of Wealth's birthday, worshippers pour in from all over Taiwan, and the temple's tradition of handing out 'fortune money' draws crowds of people hoping for prosperity.

visit.whenToGo: On lunar 3/15, the Martial God of Wealth's birthday, worshippers from everywhere pour in; the mother coins handed out over the New Year also draw many visitors.

name: Taichung Fahua Temple
address: No. 2, Juren St., West Dist., Taichung City
description: Taichung Fahua Temple, in Taichung's West District, is dedicated to Shakyamuni Buddha. It began as a mission station set up by the Nichiren school during the Japanese colonial era and was only renamed Fahua Temple after the war; its current six-story building was completed in 1996. The grounds are quiet and peaceful, a place in the middle of the busy city where you can let your mind settle.
history: Fahua Temple began in 1913, the second year of the Taisho era, as the 'Taichung Mission Station' that the Nichiren school established on Juren Street in Taichung, with the temple name Shinju-in. After the war in 1945, it was renamed Fahua Temple. In 1994, because the building had fallen into disrepair over the years, the temple rebuilt it as a six-story structure, completed in 1996. Today its main hall enshrines Shakyamuni Buddha.

visit.gettingThere: About a 9-minute walk (650 m) from Taichung Station.

name: Shanbian Mazu Temple
address: No. 108-3, Shanbian, Houlong Township, Miaoli County
description: A Mazu who for decades had no temple of her own: that is the moving devotion of Shanbian Mazu in Houlong Township, Miaoli County. Shanbian Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother) long kept the unusual tradition of 'a deity without a temple,' cared for in turn in the home of each year's appointed incense-burner host. Only in 2013 was she enthroned in a temporary temple, and a larger temple is now being planned. Shanbian Mazu and Baishatun Mazu are as close as sisters: since 1953 they have insisted on sharing a single palanquin on the pilgrimage to Beigang, and she is an indispensable part of the procession. Her palanquin is light and nimble, and often surprises the crowd with astonishing moves.
history: Because nothing was written down in the early days, the exact origins of Shanbian Mazu can no longer be traced. For a long time, Shanbian Mazu has followed the 'yearly incense-burner host' system: each year a host is chosen by casting divination blocks, and the host welcomes Mazu into their home to worship her there. This form of 'a deity without a temple' is completely different from that of the great temples. Since 1953, the 42nd year of the Republic of China, Shanbian Mazu has shared the same palanquin with the Mazu of Baishatun Gongtian Temple every year on the walking pilgrimage to Beigang Chaotian Temple, without a break for more than seventy years. In 2013, Shanbian Mazu was ritually installed in a temporary temple, but the 'host's Mazu' is still kept in the home of that year's host. Today the community is working together to build a permanent temple, so that this Mazu will finally have a home of her own.

visit.whenToGo: It draws the most attention during the annual pilgrimage, when it shares the palanquin with Baishatun Mazu and walks to Beigang Chaotian Temple. The departure date is decided each year by casting moon blocks.

name: Xiangtianhu Pasta'ay Ceremonial Ground
address: Xiangtianhu, Donghe Village, Nanzhuang Township, Miaoli County
description: The lake drifts in and out of the morning mist, and all night long a mournful, ancient ritual song echoes along its shore. This is Xiangtianhu (Lake Facing Heaven), in a mountain basin about 738 meters above sea level: the ceremonial ground of the southern group of the Saisiyat people's Pasta'ay, the Ritual of the Short Spirits (the northern group's ground is in Wufeng, Hsinchu), and the most mysterious and moving indigenous ceremonial site in Taiwan. Ringed by mountains, the scenery feels like a dream. The Pasta'ay is held as a minor ritual every two years and a grand ritual every ten. It lasts four days and three nights and runs through the night by the lake, with solemn songs and slow dance steps offering repentance, thanks, and prayers to the spirits of the ancient short people. The ritual was designated an Important Folk Custom of Taiwan in 2013, and beside the ceremonial ground stands the Saisiyat Folklore Museum, opened in 2004.
history: Legend says that in ancient times a people of small stature but enormous strength, the ta'ay, lived alongside the Saisiyat and taught them farming, song, and dance. But the ta'ay later harassed Saisiyat women again and again, until the tribe could bear it no longer and secretly tampered with the mountain-loquat-tree bridge leading to the ta'ay's home; when the ta'ay crossed, they fell and drowned. Before they died, the ta'ay laid a curse, and from then on the Saisiyat suffered failed harvests and one disaster after another. To calm the resentment of the dead and pray for good harvests, the Saisiyat began holding the Pasta'ay. The ritual songs are said to be the very ones the ta'ay taught as they were dying, their melodies mournful and ancient, a precious living fossil of oral literature. To this day, the Xiangtianhu ceremonial ground keeps this ancient ritual tradition alive, an important sacred site for passing on Saisiyat culture.

visit.whenToGo: The Pasta'ai is held as a smaller ceremony every two years and a major one every ten years, lasting four days and three nights with all-night rites by the lake. Outside the ceremony, you can visit the Saisiyat Folk Museum next door.

name: Zhunan Wugu Temple
address: No. 16, Wugu St, Zhunan Township, Miaoli County
description: Ride the train through Zhunan, glance out the window, and a 46.8-meter statue of Shennong, the Divine Farmer, suddenly appears. That is Wugu Temple. Completed in 1998, the giant statue has become the most recognizable landmark in all of Zhunan: you do not need to check the timetable, because when you see him, you know you have arrived. Its full name is the Zhunan-Toufen-Zaoqiao Wugu Temple, and it is dedicated to Shennong, the Emperor of the Five Grains, worshipped jointly by the Hoklo and Hakka communities of Zhunan, Toufen, and Zaoqiao. In an era of sharp ethnic boundaries, this kind of shared Hoklo-Hakka worship was quite rare. Shennong watches over farming and medicine, and for more than two hundred years, people here have always come to tell him first how the harvest is going.
history: In 1739, the fourth year of the Qianlong reign, Lin Ershun of Quanzhou led more than thirty settlers of Fujianese and Cantonese origin to sign an agreement with the local indigenous people to open land along the Zhonggang River, and that year they began worshipping Shennong: first came the land clearing, then the faith. In 1797, the second year of the Jiaqing reign, landholders including Zhang Zhengyang, Zhang San, and Wang Xian proposed building a temple, and Wugu Temple finally had a permanent hall. In 1851, the first year of the Xianfeng reign, an incense division went to the Sanwan Wugu Temple, and in 1874, the 13th year of the Tongzhi reign, the temple was rebuilt and a donors' stele was erected, recording the names of those who gave money and labor. In 1998 the giant Shennong statue was completed, turning a farming faith of more than two centuries into the most eye-catching landmark beside the railway.

visit.whenToGo: Shennong Dadi's birthday on lunar 4/26 is the most important celebration of the year.

name: Lugu Fenghuangshan Temple
address: No. 12-1, Miaokou Ln, Lugu Township, Nantou County
description: The god worshipped here carries the word "shame" in his name — you'd be hard pressed to find another god in Taiwan named after his own regrets. Cankui Zushi, born Pan Liaoquan, attained the Way through practice on Yinna Mountain in Guangdong. Before he died, feeling he had not managed to bring all beings across to freedom from suffering, he told his disciples to carve the words "cankui" — shame — on his stupa. Lugu Fenghuangshan Temple, built in the Jiaqing era, is the heart of Cankui Zushi worship in the Nantou mountains. For the Han settlers who came into these hills to clear land, he was the most practical of gods: malaria, wild beasts, getting lost in the mountains — he was the one they prayed to. The temple sits down a lane in Fenghuang Village, the altitude bringing a cool edge to the air, so quiet you can hear the wind from across the tea gardens.
history: Fenghuangshan Temple was built in the Jiaqing era of the Qing dynasty, just as Han settlers were pushing into the Nantou mountains. The pioneering parties carried Cankui Zushi's incense with them, because the three things most feared in the mountains — malaria, wild beasts and losing your way — were, in legend, all his to handle. When the first settlers arrived and found fertile land that looked like home, they built grass huts and stayed, enshrining the incense they had carried with them; that was the temple's earliest form. More than two hundred years on, Lugu has gone from frontier to tea country, and Fenghuangshan Temple is still the center of Cankui Zushi worship in the mountains. Every year on the Patriarch's birthday, the 16th day of the 3rd lunar month, devotees come back from all over to pay their respects, and the mountain roads fill with people.

visit.whenToGo: On lunar 3/16, Cankui Zushi's birthday, worshippers from everywhere return to pay their respects, and the mountain road is at its most crowded.
